extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, patent examiners, and litigants evaluating patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the Supreme Court's §101 framework (Mayo two-step) to determine whether claimed subject matter is a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea, and if so whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' that transforms it into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit §101 exception for laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 contains an implicit exception: 'Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas' are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion is longstanding and aims to prevent monopolization of the basic tools of scientific and technological work; citation examples include Benson, Flook, and Myriad. The court emphasizes the need to avoid granting patents that 'tie up' these building blocks and impede innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). If so, then ask whether the claim's elements, considered individually and 'as an ordered combination,' transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step two is described as a search for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept itself. (Cites Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify whether claim is directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims drawn to fundamental economic practices or methods of organizing human activity—such as hedging or intermediated settlement—are 'abstract ideas' and fall within the §101 exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treats longstanding commercial practices (e.g., hedging in Bilski; intermediated settlement in Alice) as abstract ideas. Presence of mathematical formulas is not required for a finding of abstraction; methods organizing human activity can qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claim elements individually and as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying step two, consider each element of the claim separately and then consider the elements together as an 'ordered combination' to determine whether they add enough to transform the abstract idea into an inventive application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is consistent with treating patent claims as a whole while still searching for any 'inventive concept.' The Court explicitly commands this twofold consideration (individual + ordered combination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an 'inventive concept' at Mayo step two
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites an abstract idea must include additional features—an 'inventive concept'—sufficient to ensure the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mayo held mere instructions to apply a law of nature were insufficient; Diehr was patent-eligible because the claim included steps that improved a technological process. The inventive concept must be more than conventional or routine activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating an abstract idea while adding the words 'apply it with a computer' does not make the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Benson and Flook: implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer or reciting a computer 'machine' performs no transformative work. Because computers are ubiquitous, merely using one to perform conventional functions provides no 'practical assurance' of something more than the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simply appending conventional steps at a high level is not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Simply appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality,’ to a method already well known in the art is insufficient to supply the inventive concept needed for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo emphasized that adding routine, well-understood, or conventional activities (even if described generally) does not transform an ineligible concept into an eligible application. The Court labels the computer functions in Alice (creating/maintaining records, obtaining data, adjusting balances, issuing instructions) as 'purely conventional.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that effect an improvement in technology may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that uses an abstract idea or formula but employs additional steps to solve a technological problem—thereby improving an existing technological process—can be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Diehr is cited: although Diehr used a mathematical equation, the claimed process improved rubber-curing by incorporating thermocouple measurements and repeated recalculation, thereby transforming the formula into an inventive application. Eligibility depends on actual technological improvement, not mere computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate preemption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: One concern driving the exclusion of laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas is pre-emption: patents should not monopolize fundamental tools and thereby inhibit future innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pre-emption analysis is central—if a claim would 'pre-empt use of this approach in all fields' or grant a monopoly over an abstract idea, that counsels against eligibility. The Court repeatedly frames §101 analysis with the goal of avoiding such monopolies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional, generic hardware recitations do not confer patent eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting generic computer components (e.g., 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' 'data storage unit') in functional terms that merely perform conventional calculations, storage, and transmission does not provide a meaningful limitation beyond implementing the idea on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System claims that add only generic hardware configured to perform the same abstract idea are substantively no different from method claims and fail §101 for the same reasons; the Court warns against letting 'draftsman's art' determine eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: System and media claims rise or fall with method claims when they add nothing substantive
rubrics_metrics.description: If system and computer-readable medium claims add no substantive limitation beyond the abstract idea as implemented on a generic computer, they are patent ineligible along with the method claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court notes petitioner conceded media claims rise or fall with method claims; system claims that merely recite a handful of generic components configured to implement the idea add nothing 'of substance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' while searching for inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Mayo directs courts to consider claim elements both individually and in combination, the general rule remains that patent claims must be considered as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court cites Diamond v. Diehr to emphasize consistency: one should examine claims as a whole but still perform the step-two inquiry to identify whether the combination supplies an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longstanding commercial practices are often abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that are 'fundamental economic practice[s] long prevalent in our system of commerce'—for example, hedging or using a clearing-house/intermediary—are treated as abstract ideas for §101 purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski and Alice illustrate that age or prevalence of a commercial practice supports treating it as an abstract idea rather than a patent-eligible process; historical usage (e.g., clearing-houses) is evidence of abstraction rather than novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of mathematical formula is not the sole determinant of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract-ideas category is not confined to 'preexisting, fundamental truth[s]' or mathematical formulas; methods for organizing human activity can also be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejects the argument that only formulas or scientific truths fall into the category by citing Bilski where a method of hedging (a series of steps organizing activity) was held abstract. Thus, lack of a formula does not preclude a finding of abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting claim drafting decide eligibility ('draftsman’s art')
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under §101 should not depend simply on how the claim is drafted—reciting an abstract idea in different words or attaching generic technological labels should not render it eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court warns that interpreting §101 to permit claims that merely rephrase abstract ideas or tack on conventional computer language would 'make patent eligibility depend simply on the draftsman’s art' and eviscerate the exclusion for abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-method claims may be ineligible as non-§101 'processes'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'merely describe a method of doing business' may not qualify as a 'process' under §101 and thus can be patent-ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Sotomayor's concurrence (citing Bilski) reiterates that organizing human activity/business methods are typically not processes under §101. This guidance supports treating business-method patents skeptically under the abstract-idea framework.
